title: The partly column
hookLine: modern writers, not Epictetus, add a third column: things partly up to me

cards: Try Epictetus's two columns on a real worry, and something awkward happens. Say you're worried about your health. Is it up to you?
Not entirely: genes, accidents, luck. Not up to you at all? That doesn't feel right either.
You choose what you eat, whether you walk, whether you see a doctor. Or your kid's grades. Your marriage.
Your job. Plenty of what people actually lie awake about doesn't fit neatly in either column. It sits somewhere in between.

teach.b: First, the honest history. Epictetus had two columns, not three.
The third was added in modern times, notably by the American philosophy professor William Irvine in a 2009 book on Stoic practice.
He called it the trichotomy of control: things we have complete control over, things we have no control over, and things we have some control over. Some Stoic scholars push back.
Epictetus didn't need a third column, they say, because anything partly up to you can be split into the part that's yours and the part that isn't.
Here's the useful thing: follow either path carefully and you end up in the same place. Take the tennis match, Irvine's own example.
Winning is partly up to you; you can't control your opponent, the wind or the line judge.
So you break the partly column open and look for the piece that's fully yours: to practice hard, and play as well as you can today. That becomes your goal. Not win, but play my best.
Which is exactly Cato's archer from yesterday, aiming well and letting the result go. The partly column isn't a place to leave things. It's a place to open them up.

teach.h: FIND THE PIECE THAT'S FULLY YOURS.
teach.b: Your health: the walk, the vegetables, the appointment are yours; the rest is not. Your kid's grades: the quiet desk, the encouragement, the patience are yours; the grades are theirs.
Find your part. Do your part. Let the rest be the rest.

how: Some modern readers of Stoicism use a three-column sort, following William Irvine: what's fully up to me, what isn't, and what's partly up to me, which they break down until they find the piece that is fully theirs.

o: a split of the soul into three separate parts
a third column for what's partly up to you
three rules Epictetus gave for any hard choice

games.q: what's inside the partly column — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus taught three columns of control
he had two. the third was added in our own time, notably by William Irvine.
some scholars say the third column isn't needed
anything partly yours can be split into the part that's yours and the part that isn't.
the partly column is where you park worries you can't sort
it's a place to break things open and find the piece that is fully yours.

games.q: you're about to play a tennis match and you badly want to win. using the partly column, what do you set as your goal?
o: don't care about the result at all.
play as well as you can today.
games.why: winning is only partly yours. playing your best is fully yours, so that becomes the goal. it's the archer again.

practice: Hold one thing you care about that's partly up to you, your health, a relationship, a project, and break it open: what, in this, is fully mine? Maybe one call, one habit, one kind word, one hour; name it clearly.
Then set the rest down beside it, gently, not mine, and breathe with your part in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Trichotomy. William Irvine's name for the third column, what's partly up to you, broken open to find the piece that's fully yours. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my part only. Even big, tangled things have a piece that's yours. Day one hundred thirteen, done.

sources.ref: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy (2009), chapter on the trichotomy of control
